He may have studied languages, music, or medicine, particularly when a member of his family entrusted him to an experienced teacher. His departure may result from a mission to carry a message to the Dúnedain, the search for an ancient manuscript, or the desire to discover human communities he knows only through stories. The encounters he experiences will allow him to understand how greatly the obligations, customs, and concerns of mortals differ from those of his Elven surroundings.

Another character may have grown up in a Dúnadan family, where his Elven ancestry is known to those close to him but remains relatively discreet in dealings with strangers. He has received weapons training, participated in defending the land, or learned to understand the responsibilities attached to his name. His companions nevertheless age more quickly than he does, and he gradually begins to appreciate the consequences of his constitution. He may have known several generations of neighbours, preserve memories of ancient chiefs, and observe family responsibilities passing from one person to another while he remains personally involved in the affairs of his community. His departure may be prompted by a mission entrusted to him by a relative, the search for an inheritance, or the need to protect a family to which he remains bound by ancient obligations.

A woman of mixed ancestry may belong to a house whose members have maintained relations with an Elven refuge for several generations. She travels to carry messages, gather information, or negotiate agreements between communities. Her knowledge of languages and traditions represents a valuable advantage, particularly when she must understand ancient documents or explain the customs of one people to those unfamiliar with them. Her activities may also place considerable family responsibilities upon her, especially when several lineages expect her to honour commitments made long before her birth. She may wish to continue this role as a mediator, but may equally seek a different existence devoted to a trade or studies she has personally chosen.

A character born of a recent union between an Elf and a Man occupies a more uncertain position, particularly when he does not belong to the celebrated lineages. His birth may have been welcomed by both families, but historical circumstances may also lead his relatives to preserve a measure of discretion concerning his origins. He may grow up in a community that knows his ancestry perfectly well, or discover only later in life the history of one of his parents. The nature of his destiny must then be established with the Gamemaster, without assuming that the Choice automatically belongs to him. His adventure may arise from the desire to understand his origins, find a parent, or study the traditions of a community whose connections with his family he is only gradually discovering.

The question of the Choice, when it genuinely applies to a character, may occupy a central place in his history. It may remain a distant concern, have already been answered, or gradually become more important as personal relationships and events lead him to reflect upon his destiny. He must then consider the practical consequences of belonging to the Eldar or to Men, particularly the people among whom he wishes to remain and the commitments he intends to preserve. Such reflection may be nourished by the counsel of loved ones, the tales of Elrond and Elros, or experiences gained alongside mortal companions. It must not, however, become a decision the character may freely reverse according to the advantages he expects to gain, since the Choice constitutes an irrevocable commitment whose conditions must be clearly established before the campaign begins.

This singularity should not reduce his whole existence to a melancholy period of waiting. A Half-elf may find profound joy in his work, enjoy the company of friends, pursue adventure out of curiosity, or devote several years to perfecting an art. He may be impatient, generous, ambitious, proud, or possess a temperament entirely different from that expected of a descendant of the ancient houses. Some seek travel and new encounters, while others prefer to remain in a community whose customs they know intimately. Long life may nourish patience and prudence, but may also encourage boldness when the character believes he possesses the experience needed to undertake a difficult task.

The choice of occupation provides an essential source of roleplaying possibilities. A Peredhel may have received craft training under an Elven master, learned medical techniques within a Dúnadan household, or helped administer a human estate. He may cultivate the land, forge weapons, study ancient languages, or maintain the roads and structures of a settlement. Such occupations give his life tangible concerns, particularly when he must reconcile professional responsibilities with the expectations of his family. A character may possess remarkable experience in one particular field while remaining largely ignorant of others, for longevity and ancestry grant no universal mastery of knowledge.

Relations with other peoples may also transform his convictions. A Half-elf raised within an Elven community may discover among Men an understanding of time and responsibility whose significance he had never fully appreciated, while another, accustomed to human institutions, gradually learns to understand the patience of the Eldar. The knowledge of the Khazâd may reveal techniques unknown to his teachers, while the Hobbits show him a way of life principally devoted to family and ordinary occupations. Such encounters may change his understanding of ancient alliances, lead him to overcome a prejudice, or strengthen a loyalty whose value he now better appreciates. His dual ancestry sometimes favours a particular understanding of cultural differences, but guarantees neither impartiality nor the ability to resolve every conflict.

The professional possibilities of the Peredhil reflect this diversity. A Fighter may have received training in human armies or among the defenders of an Elven refuge, while a Ranger possesses knowledge acquired through patrols and journeys in the wilderness. A Rogue may have developed his abilities during discreet missions, negotiations, or travels requiring great caution, while a Bard may devote his life to the tales, languages, and musical traditions of both peoples. Scholarly paths, healing, and certain magical Professions may also be considered according to the compatibilities and restrictions established by MERP-UI. A Half-elf's heritage may explain his dispositions and the teachings to which he has had access, but the skills and spells he masters must remain consistent with his training and RMU rules.

The choice of Age is ultimately decisive. At the end of the First Age, a character may belong to the earliest unions between Elves and Men or live among the survivors of the kingdoms of Beleriand, provided his origins are consistent with historical events. During the Second Age, he may move among Elven communities and Númenórean settlements, while the lineages of Elrond and Elros pursue their now divergent destinies. During the Third Age, he may maintain relations with Rivendell, the Dúnedain, or the other Free Peoples, particularly in the context of the long wars against Sauron. During the Fourth Age, he may take part in rebuilding the kingdoms, preserve the knowledge of earlier times, or continue his existence in a world where the presence of the Eldar is gradually becoming less conspicuous. Each period influences the unions that are possible, the generations already born, and the events the character may personally remember.

The Half-elves — Peredhil Race is available in MERP-UI at the end of the First Age, and subsequently during the Second, Third, and Fourth Ages of Middle-earth, subject to suitable historical justification. It remains restricted in every Age, for unions between Elves and Men are exceptionally rare and their representation carries important consequences for genealogy, longevity, and the destiny of characters. The choice of a Culture defines the community in which the character grew up, the languages he knows, the traditions to which he belongs, and the skills acquired during his training. A Peredhel raised among the Sindar does not necessarily possess the same knowledge as another who grew up within a Dúnadan household, even when their racial dispositions are comparable.

Before approving the creation of a Half-elven character, the player and Gamemaster should establish the identity or origins of his parents, any connection with a recognised lineage, the community that raised him, and the nature of his destiny. They must also determine whether the character genuinely possesses the privilege of the Choice, whether that decision has already been made, and what its consequences will be. These elements preserve the consistency of his history with Tolkien's traditions and the developments adopted from MERP, without altering existing RMU mechanics. The character must then be given a personal life: a family, a trade, companions, commitments, and aspirations whose consequences will unfold during his adventures.

A Peredhel inherits the legacy of two peoples whose histories have been intertwined since the earliest Ages of Middle-earth. His ancestry may grant him access to ancient knowledge, exceptional relationships, and, in certain lineages alone, the privilege of choosing his destiny. Yet the singularity of his birth determines neither the commitments he will accept nor the works to which he will devote his life. The people he chooses to love, the responsibilities he decides to assume, and the deeds he accomplishes will give true meaning to the heritages he has received, whether he ultimately shares the fate of the Eldar or that of Men.
